title: CSS Selectors, the Cascade, and Boxes
summary: Learn how the browser decides which rule wins for every element, and how each element becomes a box with content, padding, border, and margin.
intro: CSS is how a page gets its colors, fonts, and spacing, and it's where beginners lose the most time: a rule that does nothing, a color that won't change however many times you set it, a box that's wider than the width you gave it. None of that is random. The browser follows a few exact rules to decide which of your declarations applies to each element, and to work out how big each element's box is. This lesson teaches those rules: how CSS gets into a page, how selectors pick elements, how the cascade picks a winner when rules disagree, how values pass down the tree, how every element becomes a box, and the units you'll size boxes with. You'll style the bakery's pages as you go.

examples.title: Linking a stylesheet
examples.prompt: In your `bakery` folder, make a `css` folder holding `style.css`, put the reset above at the top, then these rules after it. Add `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/style.css">` to the head of `recipe.html`, and open it.
examples.explanation: The page now uses the Georgia font, with more space between lines, and the main heading turns brown. The `h2` headings stay black, because `colour` isn't a CSS property: CSS uses the American spelling. The browser skipped that one declaration without a word. Click an `h2` in the Elements tab, and the Styles pane shows the rule from `style.css` with `colour` struck through and a warning sign, beside the user agent stylesheet's rule for `h2`. Fix the spelling, save, and reload. `font-family` lists fonts in order of preference: Georgia if the computer has it, and if not, any font with serifs, the small strokes on the ends of letters.

steps.title: Selectors
steps.body:
A selector is how a rule says which elements it's for. Choose it well, and your styles land exactly where you meant, without touching anything else. The handful of selectors in this part cover nearly everything you'll write.

## The basic selectors

| Selector | Picks | Example |
|---|---|---|
| type | every element of that type | `p`, `h2`, `button` |
| class | every element with that class | `.price` |
| id | the one element with that id | `#order-form` |
| attribute | elements with that attribute, or that value | `[required]`, `[type="email"]` |
| universal | every element | `*` |

Classes are what you'll use most. They say what something is in your design, like `.price` or `.card`, and any number of elements can share one. Ids are unique, so a rule written for an id can never be reused, and the next part shows a second reason to keep them out of selectors.

Attribute selectors have a few variations. `[href^="https"]` picks links whose address starts with `https`, and `[href$=".pdf"]` those that end in `.pdf`.

Join selectors with no space to require both: `button.primary` picks buttons that also have the class `primary`. Join them with commas to give several selectors the same declarations: `h1, h2, h3` picks all three kinds of heading.

## Combinators

A **combinator** picks elements by where they sit in the tree, relative to another element:

- A space: `nav a` picks every `a` anywhere inside a `nav`, however deep. This one is called the **descendant** combinator.
- `>`: `ul > li` picks only an `li` whose parent is that `ul`. That's the **child** combinator.
- `+`: `h2 + p` picks a `p` that comes straight after an `h2`, with the same parent.
- `~`: `h2 ~ p` picks every `p` that comes after an `h2`, with the same parent.

## Pseudo-classes: elements in a state

A **pseudo-class**, written with one colon, picks elements by their state or their place, things the HTML doesn't spell out:

- `:hover` matches while the pointer is over the element.
- `:focus-visible` matches when the element has focus and the browser thinks a focus ring should show, which it does for the keyboard but not for most clicks. Style focus with it, never take it away.
- `:checked`, `:disabled`, and `:user-invalid` match form fields in those states.
- `:first-child` and `:last-child` match an element that's the first or last child of its parent.
- `:nth-child()` matches by position: `:nth-child(3)` is the third, `:nth-child(odd)` is the first, third, fifth, and so on, and `:nth-child(3n)` is every third.
- `:not()` matches elements that don't match what's inside it: `li:not(:last-child)` is every item but the last.

## Pseudo-elements: parts of an element

A **pseudo-element**, written with two colons, styles a part of an element as if it were an element of its own:

- `::before` and `::after` add a piece of content at the start or end of the element. They need a `content` property to appear, like `content: "→ "`.
- `::first-line` is the first line of a paragraph, however wide the screen.
- `::placeholder` is a field's placeholder text, and `::marker` is a list item's bullet or number.

## Grouping with :is, :where, and :has

- `:is()` matches anything in its list, which shortens long selectors: `:is(h1, h2, h3) a` instead of `h1 a, h2 a, h3 a`.
- `:where()` does exactly the same, with one difference the next part explains: it adds nothing to a selector's strength.
- `:has()` matches an element by what's inside it, or what comes after it. `.card:has(img)` picks cards that contain a picture. `label:has(:checked)` picks a label whose box is ticked. `form:has(:user-invalid)` picks a form with a problem anywhere in it. CSS never had a way to style an element based on its children before, and it's Baseline Widely available now.

## Reading a selector

Browsers read a selector from right to left. In `nav li > a:hover`, the browser first finds links being hovered, then keeps those whose parent is an `li`, then keeps those inside a `nav`. Reading it the same way helps you: the selector's last piece says which elements get the style, and everything before it narrows them down.

examples.title: Styling the menu
examples.prompt: Add these rules to `style.css`, and add `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/style.css">` to the head of `home.html` too. Open it, move your pointer over the links, then press Tab to move between them.
examples.explanation: The menu's list loses its bullets and its indent, and `display: inline` sets its items side by side, like words in a line. `nav li + li` picks every item that comes straight after another one, so all but the first, and `::before` puts a divider at the start of each, giving Breads | Cakes. Hovering a menu link turns it brown. Tab to a link and it gets a thick orange outline, while clicking with a mouse shows none. Open Opening hours, and two things change. `[open]` is an attribute selector: browsers add `open` to a `<details>` while it's open, so its summary turns bold. And `main:has(details[open]) h1` picks the heading of a `main` that holds an open details, so the heading turns green. Close it, and both go back. The heading changed because of something elsewhere on the page, which only `:has()` can do.

steps.title: Specificity and the cascade
steps.body:
Sooner or later two rules set the same property on the same element, and only one can win. The **cascade** is the set of rules the browser uses to pick the winner. Once you know it, you stop guessing, and you stop piling on stronger and stronger selectors to force a style through.

## When rules collide

A collision is about one property on one element. If one rule sets an `h2`'s color and another sets its font size, both apply, and there's no contest. Only when two declarations set the same property on the same element does the browser need to choose. It compares them in steps, and the first step that tells them apart decides:

```diagram css-cascade-and-boxes-cascade
Each step only matters when the steps before it end in a tie.
```

1. **Origin and importance.** Where the declaration came from: the browser's own stylesheet, or yours. Yours beat the browser's. A declaration marked `!important` beats every normal one, wherever it came from.
2. **The style attribute.** A declaration in an element's `style` attribute beats any rule from a stylesheet.
3. **Layers.** Rules can be sorted into named layers, and a later layer beats an earlier one. More on these below.
4. **Specificity.** The more specific selector wins.
5. **Order.** When everything else ties, the declaration that comes last wins. Within a file that means further down, and across files, the stylesheet linked later.

Most collisions you'll meet are settled at step 4 or 5.

## Specificity

**Specificity** is a selector's strength, counted in three columns, written like (1, 0, 2):

- **Ids**: how many id selectors it has.
- **Classes**: how many classes, attribute selectors, and pseudo-classes.
- **Types**: how many type selectors and pseudo-elements.

The universal selector `*` and the combinators count nothing. Compare two selectors column by column, from the left, and the first column that differs decides. One id beats any number of classes, and one class beats any number of types.

| Selector | Specificity |
|---|---|
| `p` | (0, 0, 1) |
| `nav a` | (0, 0, 2) |
| `.price` | (0, 1, 0) |
| `p.price` | (0, 1, 1) |
| `nav a:hover` | (0, 1, 2) |
| `.menu .price` | (0, 2, 0) |
| `#special` | (1, 0, 0) |

`:is()`, `:not()`, and `:has()` count as the most specific selector inside them. `:where()` always counts zero, whatever is inside it, which makes it perfect for defaults that anything should be able to override. DevTools shows a selector's specificity when you hover over it in the Styles pane.

This is the second reason to keep ids out of your CSS. A rule like `#menu a` is so strong that any later rule for those links needs an id too, and every fix makes the next one harder.

## Layers

A big stylesheet has kinds of rules that should always beat others, whatever their selectors: a reset should lose to everything, and a small helper class like `.hidden` should beat everything. **Cascade layers** let you say so. Name the layers once, in order, at the top of your CSS, and then put rules in them:

```css
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

@layer base {
  .menu a { color: saddlebrown; }
}

@layer utilities {
  .muted { color: gray; }
}
```

Later layers win, so a link with the class `muted` in the menu is gray. Without the layers, `.menu a`, at (0, 1, 1), would beat `.muted`, at (0, 1, 0), and the link would stay brown. Specificity still decides between rules inside the same layer. And any CSS that isn't in a layer at all beats every layer, so a stylesheet can adopt layers one piece at a time.

## Why to avoid !important

`!important`, written after a value, like `color: gray !important`, jumps a declaration over almost everything. It's tempting when a style won't apply. But the only thing that beats it is another `!important`, so it starts a race nobody wins, and the stylesheet grows harder to change with every one.

When a rule loses, find out why in the Styles pane, then fix the cause: put the rule later, give it one more class, or move the rules into layers. Keep `!important` for the rare rule that truly must never lose, like a helper class that hides things.

examples.title: Who wins
examples.prompt: Four rules for the same paragraph. Save the page as `cascade.html` in `bakery` and open it. Then delete the rules one at a time, from the top, reloading each time, and watch the color change.
examples.code: Sourdough loaf: 3.50
examples.explanation: All four rules match the paragraph, so all four set its color, and the browser goes through the steps. They come from the same origin, none is in a style attribute or a layer, so specificity decides. `#special` is (1, 0, 0), the strongest, so the text starts green. Delete it, and `.menu .price`, at (0, 2, 0), beats `.price`, at (0, 1, 0), so it turns blue, even though `.price` comes later. Delete that, and crimson wins, then gray, which is the weakest, at (0, 0, 1), and only won because nothing else was left. Before you delete anything, check the Styles pane: it lists all four, with every loser's color struck through.

steps.title: Inheritance, custom properties, and nesting

examples.title: The bakery's tokens
examples.prompt: Put these rules near the top of `style.css`, after the reset, and delete the `h1` rule from the first example, since the heading now takes its color from a token. Then add `class="sale"` to the `<main>` of `home.html` and reload.
examples.explanation: The page's text is now a soft black, `#222`, a color written in hex, which the last part of this lesson explains. It's set once on the `body` and inherited by everything inside it. The menu's links and the main heading are both brown, from one shared token. Adding `class="sale"` to `<main>` turns the heading red and adds (sale!) after it, while the menu stays brown: `.sale` sets `--brand` again only inside `<main>`, and every `var(--brand)` in there now reads crimson. The nested rule is `.sale h1::after`. Look at the `h1` in the Computed pane, and `color` shows the final crimson value, with the rule that set it.

steps.title: The box model
steps.body:
Every element on a page is drawn as a rectangle, a box, which you met in the lesson on how a browser draws a page. Every box is made of the same four layers. Knowing them is what lets you add space exactly where you want it, and explains the classic surprise of a box coming out wider than the width you gave it.

## Four layers

From the inside out:

- The **content**: the text or picture itself. `width` and `height` set its size.
- The **padding**: space between the content and the border, filled with the element's background.
- The **border**: a line around the padding, which can have its own width, style, and color.
- The **margin**: space outside the border, which keeps other boxes away. It's always see-through.

```diagram css-cascade-and-boxes-box
A 300 pixel wide card with 20 pixels of padding and a 2 pixel border is 344 pixels wide, unless box-sizing changes the sum.
```

Each can be set for one side or all four: `padding: 20px` sets all four sides, `padding-top` only the top, and `padding: 10px 20px` sets the top and bottom to 10 pixels and the sides to 20. A border takes a width, a style, and a color: `border: 2px solid saddlebrown`. Margin works like padding.

## Where the width goes

By default, `width` sets the content's width alone. Padding and border are added around it. So a card with `width: 300px`, `padding: 20px`, and `border: 2px solid` takes up 300 + 20 + 20 + 2 + 2 = 344 pixels across, as the diagram shows. That's surprising when all you wanted was a 300 pixel card, and it's worse with a width like `100%`: the box comes out wider than its parent, and pokes out of it.

`box-sizing: border-box` changes the sum. The width then includes the padding and the border, and the content shrinks to make room. The same card is exactly 300 pixels across, with 256 pixels left for its content. That's far easier to work with, which is why the reset in the first part sets it on every element. The default is called `content-box`.

The Computed pane draws the box model for any element you select, with its four layers and their sizes. Hover over each layer, and the page highlights it.

## Margins that collapse

Paragraphs have a margin of 16 pixels above and below them, from the user agent stylesheet. So you might expect 32 pixels between two paragraphs, 16 from each. There are only 16. When the bottom margin of one block touches the top margin of the next, they **collapse** into one margin, as big as the larger of the two.

It's meant to keep spacing even in ordinary text. But it surprises people in a second form. When the first child's top margin touches its parent's top edge, with no padding or border in between, it collapses through the parent, and pushes the parent down instead. A heading at the top of a card seems to move the whole card. Margins don't collapse once anything stands between them, like a little padding or a border on the parent, or inside the layouts the next CSS lesson covers, flexbox and grid.

## Outline is not border

An **outline** is drawn outside the border, but unlike a border, it takes up no space at all. Adding one never moves anything on the page. That's why browsers draw focus rings as outlines: a ring that pushed things around every time you pressed Tab would make the page jump. Use `outline` for focus styles, and add `outline-offset` to leave a small gap between the ring and the element.

## Inline boxes

Inline elements, like a link or a `<strong>` in a paragraph, have boxes too, but their padding and margin work only partly. Side to side, they push the words around them apart. Up and down, the background grows, but the lines of text around it don't move. To give something in a line of text a real height, change its `display`, which the next CSS lesson covers.

examples.title: Two cards, two sums
examples.prompt: Save this as `boxes.html` in `bakery` and open it. Both cards say `width: 300px`. Click each one in the Elements tab and look at the box model drawing in the Computed pane.
examples.code:
content-box: 344px across
border-box: 300px across
examples.explanation: The first card is wider than the second, though both have the same `width`. In the Computed pane, the first card's box model shows 300 in the middle, 20 on each side for padding, and 2 for the border, so 344 in all. The second shows 256 in the middle: the browser shrank the content so that content, padding, and border add up to 300. The gap between the cards is 16 pixels, not 32, because the first card's bottom margin and the second card's top margin collapse into one. Hover over the margin in the drawing and the page shows that single gap.

steps.title: Units and values
steps.body:
Every size and color in CSS is a value with a unit, and the unit decides what it's measured against: the screen, the text size, or the box around it. Picking the right one is the difference between a page that fits any screen and any text size, and one that breaks when someone zooms in.

## Pixels

`px` is the unit you've seen so far. A CSS pixel isn't one of the screen's physical dots: as the part on pictures in the HTML lesson showed, a dense screen packs two or three of those into each CSS pixel. A CSS pixel is about the same size to your eye on every screen, so `16px` text looks much the same on a phone and on a laptop.

## Sizes that follow the text

- `rem` is the font size of the root element, `html`. Browsers set that to 16 pixels unless the person has chosen bigger text in their settings. So `1rem` is 16 pixels for most people, and more for people who need it. Sizing text and spacing in `rem` respects that choice, and it's the best default for font sizes.
- `em` is the font size of the element itself. So `padding: 0.5em` on a button grows with the button's text. In `font-size` itself, `em` means the parent's font size, so `font-size: 1.5em` is half as big again as the text around it.
- `ch` is the width of the digit 0 in the current font. `max-width: 65ch` keeps lines of text to about 65 characters, a comfortable length to read.

## Sizes that follow the box or the screen

- `%` is a share of something else, which depends on the property. For `width`, it's the width of the parent's content. For `font-size`, it's the parent's font size.
- `vw` and `vh` are one hundredth of the viewport's width and height. `50vw` is half the window's width, as in the `sizes` attribute from the HTML lesson.
- On phones, the address bar slides away as you scroll, so the viewport's height changes. `svh` is a hundredth of the small height, with the bar showing, `lvh` of the large one, without it, and `dvh` follows it as it changes. `min-height: 100svh` makes a section fill the screen without hiding under the bar.

## Doing sums

Three functions work out a value from others:

- `calc()` does arithmetic, even with different units: `width: calc(100% - 2rem)` is the parent's width, less two root font sizes.
- `min()` takes the smallest of its values: `width: min(100%, 60rem)` is the full width on small screens, but never more than 60rem.
- `max()` takes the largest: `padding: max(1rem, 3vw)` grows with the screen, but never shrinks below 1rem.

## Colors

CSS has several ways to write a color:

- **Names**, like `saddlebrown`, `crimson`, and `white`. There are about 150. Every example after this one writes the same color, saddlebrown, another way.
- **Hex**, like `#8b4513`: a `#` and three pairs of hexadecimal digits, 0 to 9 then a to f, for the red, green, and blue in the color. `#222` is short for `#222222`.
- **`rgb()`**, the same red, green, and blue as numbers from 0 to 255: `rgb(139 69 19)`.
- **`hsl()`**: a hue as an angle around a color wheel, then how vivid it is and how light, as percentages: `hsl(25 76% 31%)`.
- **`oklch()`**: lightness, chroma (how vivid), and hue: `oklch(47.1% 0.112 50.8)`. It's built to match how people see, so two colors with the same lightness really do look equally light, which `hsl()` can't promise. It's the best choice for building a set of colors that work together, and it's Baseline Widely available.

Any of them can be partly see-through, with a slash and an amount, called **alpha**: `rgb(0 0 0 / 50%)` is black at half strength.

## Computed and used values

The value you write isn't always the one the browser draws with. Say a paragraph has `width: 50%` and `font-size: 1.25rem`. Its **computed value**, after the cascade and inheritance, turns what it can into absolute numbers: `font-size` becomes 20 pixels, while the width stays 50%, since a percentage can't be turned into pixels until layout. The **used value** is what's left after layout: 50% of a 640 pixel parent is 320 pixels. The Computed pane in DevTools shows the final pixel value, which is usually the one you need when something comes out the wrong size.

With selectors, the cascade, boxes, and units, you can style any one element. The next lesson puts the boxes in place, and lays out whole pages.

examples.title: Units on the bakery page
examples.prompt: Add these rules to `style.css`, and open `recipe.html`. Then raise your browser's default font size in its settings, and reload.
examples.explanation: `font-size: 100%` on `html` keeps the person's chosen size, 16 pixels unless they've changed it. The text column is now at most 65 characters wide, centered by `margin: 0 auto`, which shares the space left over equally on both sides. Its padding is 3% of the window's width, but never under 1rem. The main heading is 2.5 times the root size, 40 pixels. The `--brand` token is set again, to the same brown written in `oklch()`, and since this rule comes later it wins, so everything that uses the token keeps its color. Give any paragraph `class="note"`, and it gets a brown background at one tenth strength. Raise the default font size in your browser's settings, and every size written in `rem`, `em`, or `ch` grows with it, the column's width included.

recap:
- Put CSS in a linked stylesheet, and start it with a small reset over the browser's own styles.
- A rule is a selector and declarations, and a declaration the browser can't read is skipped without a word.
- Selectors pick by type, class, id, attribute, place in the tree, state, and even by what's inside.
- When declarations collide, the cascade checks origin and importance, the style attribute, layers, specificity, then order.
- Specificity counts ids, then classes, then types, and :where() counts zero.
- Text properties inherit and box properties don't, and custom properties inherit too, so tokens set once apply everywhere.
- A box is content, padding, border, and margin, and box-sizing: border-box makes width include the padding and border.
- rem follows the person's text size, em the element's, and oklch() writes colors the way people see them.
